question: A 24-year-old woman presents to her primary care doctor with a lesion on her labia. She first noticed the lesion 2 days ago. It is not painful. She denies vaginal discharge or dysuria. She has no past medical history and takes no medications. She has had 4 sexual partners in the past 8 months and uses the pull-out method as contraception. She drinks 12-16 alcoholic beverages per week and is a law student. Her temperature is 97.8°F (36.6°C), blood pressure is 121/81 mmHg, pulse is 70/min, and respirations are 16/min. On exam, she has an indurated non-tender ulcer on the left labia majora. There is no appreciable inguinal lymphadenopathy. Multiple tests are ordered and pending. This patient's condition is most likely caused by a pathogen with which of the following characteristics on histologic imaging?

options.opa: Gram-negative coccobacillus with a "school of fish" appearance
options.ope: Vaginal epithelial cells covered with bacteria

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Sexual contact with multiple partners -> increased risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) -> 80% CHAIN: Indurated non-tender ulcer on labia majora -> suggestive of genital ulcer disease -> 85% CHAIN: Lesion not painful -> characteristic of syphilis primary chancre -> 90% CHAIN: Syphilis primary chancre -> caused by Treponema pallidum -> 95% CHAIN: Pathogen causing syphilis primary chancre -> spirochete bacteria -> 95% CHAIN: Spirochete bacteria on histologic imaging -> motile and helical-shaped bacteria -> 80%
analysis: Based on the clinical presentation of an indurated non-tender ulcer on the labia majora in a sexually active young woman, the most likely diagnosis is genital herpes caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV). HSV infection typically presents with ulcerative lesions and can be confirmed on histologic imaging by the presence of multinucleated giant cells and intranuclear inclusions.
